# Optimizing the raw moment width over source mass does not select a deep point

This is an exact counterexample to a source-body selector, not to OC.
For an integer base j and feasible mass t>0, let M_t(j) be the interval
of continuous centroids of densities 0<=f<=1 on the mixed source having
mass t and integer-base centroid j. Set Q_t(j)=t M_t(j), the interval
of their unnormalized continuous first moments. Consider either rule:

1. At every j, maximize the length of Q_t(j) over all feasible t, take
   the midpoint of M_t(j), and choose any of the resulting points.
2. Maximize the length jointly over j and t and take that midpoint.

Both rules can fail depth 1/4, even with positive concave interval
widths and with marginal eligibility imposed on the selected base.
Allowing t to vary therefore does not repair fixed-mass midpoint selection.

## 1. Body and exact simultaneous optimization problem

Take integer bases 0,1,2,3 and fibers

    K_i=[-w_i,0],        w=(2,16,17,1).

The consecutive differences 14,1,-16 decrease. Piecewise affine
interpolation of w is concave, so these are precisely the integer
fibers of a full-dimensional convex body. Total mixed length is M=36.
The marginal median bases are 1 and 2: the prefix through 1 and suffix
through 2 both have mass 18.

For fixed source masses p_i in the fibers, the maximum continuous
first moment is -sum p_i^2/2, attained by upper subintervals. For masses
q_i the maximum negative first moment is sum(w_i q_i-q_i^2/2), attained
by lower subintervals. Endpoint rearrangement proves these assertions
for every dominated measurable density, not just interval selections.
Consequently maximizing the raw moment width over t is exactly the
strictly concave quadratic program

    maximize Phi(p,q)=-sum p_i^2/2 + sum(w_i q_i-q_i^2/2),

    0<=p_i,q_i<=w_i,
    sum p_i=sum q_i,
    sum(i-j)p_i=sum(i-j)q_i=0.                         (1)

The common mass t is recovered as sum p_i. The compact feasible set
contains zero, but its optimum has positive value and mass. Strict
concavity makes its maximizing pair unique. At that pair define

    A=-sum p_i^2/2,  B=sum(w_i q_i-q_i^2/2),
    Q_t(j)=[-B,A],   y=(A-B)/(2t).                    (2)

## 2. Exact optimizers at all four bases

At j=0, base balance forces all mass into fiber 0. The unique optimizer
has p_0=q_0=1, hence t=1, width 1, and y=-1. At j=3 it forces all mass
into fiber 3, giving p_3=q_3=1/2, width 1/4, and y=-1/2.

At j=1 the unique optimizer is

    p=(2,31/4,2,0),       q=(7/4,33/4,7/4,0).

It has

    t=47/4, A=-1089/32, B=4101/32,
    |Q_t(1)|=753/8,      y=-2595/376.                 (3)

Here is an exact global certificate. The objective gradients are
`g_p=-p` and `g_q=w-q`. Subtract the affine equality multipliers

    g_p: lambda+nu(i-j),
    g_q: -lambda+omega(i-j),

with lambda=-31/4, nu=23/4, omega=15/2. The resulting residuals are

    p: (23/2,0,0,-15/4),
    q: (0,0,0,-87/4).

Every positive residual is at an upper bound, every negative residual
at a zero bound, and free coordinates have zero residual. For every
feasible variation the equality-multiplier terms cancel and the
residual scalar product is nonpositive. The exact quadratic expansion
adds `-(|p-p*|^2+|q-q*|^2)/2`, so equality forces this optimizer.

At j=2 the unique optimizer is

    p=(0,1,8,1),         q=(0,1/2,9,1/2).

Here t=10, A=-33, B=483/4, so

    |Q_t(2)|=351/4,      y=-123/16.                   (4)

Use lambda=-8, nu=-7, omega=-15/2 in the same certificate. The
residuals are

    p: (-6,0,0,14),
    q: (-21,0,0,0).

Their bound signs again prove global optimality and uniqueness.
In particular the joint raw-width maximum is uniquely at base 1,
because 753/8>351/4>1>1/4. Base 1 is a marginal median.

## 3. Every optimized candidate has a bad closed ambient cap

At the selected point (1,-2595/376), use the closed halfspace

    H={x-100(z-1)>=-2595/376}.

It contains the whole fiber 0, cuts fiber 1 in its upper interval of
length 2595/376, and misses fibers 2 and 3. Thus

    mu(H)=2+2595/376=3347/376,
    M/4-mu(H)=37/376>0.                              (5)

At base 2, the optimized point is (2,-123/16). The halfspace
`x+100(z-2)>=-123/16` cuts its own upper interval and contains only
fiber 3 in addition. Its mass is 123/16+1=139/16<9, with deficit 5/16.

At bases 0 and 3, sufficiently large outward integer tilts isolate
half of that endpoint fiber, giving masses 1 and 1/2, respectively.
Thus even choosing the best among ALL four mass-optimized midpoints
cannot reach 1/4. Every displayed point belongs to its actual fiber.
Every halfspace is closed and nonvertical, so its boundary has zero
mixed length.

This disproves the free-mass maximum raw moment width/John interval
selector and its median-restricted version. It does not bound the
best depth in the original fibers or the best choice of point in an
entire moment interval.
